summary.text: For the three exceptional exponents, the congruence \(10^i\equiv1+9i\pmod{27,81}\), applied to a number and its reversal, forces the digit sum of any smaller common multiple to be divisible by \(27\) or \(81\); the digit-count bound then forces every digit to be \(9\), proving the required minima (with the case \(9\) immediate). For \(n\ge5\), repeat the block \(4899999987\) exactly \(T=3^{n-5}\) times: its reversal repeats \(7899999984\), both are divisible by \(3^n\) because each block value contains \(3^5\) and lifting the exponent gives \(3^{n-5}\mid\sum_{i<T}10^{10i}\), while its \(10T\) digits make it strictly smaller than the all-nines number with \(27T\) digits.

full_proof.text:
Let \(R(x)\) denote the integer obtained by reversing the decimal digits of \(x\) (initial zeroes produced by the reversal are, as usual, discarded). For a positive integer \(m\), the quantity \(a(m)\) is the least positive multiple \(x\) of \(m\) for which \(m\mid R(x)\), if such an \(x\) exists. Equivalently, it is the least number \(km\), with \(k\geq 1\), such that \(m\mid R(km)\). Thus, whenever a positive integer \(x\) satisfies
\[
 m\mid x\qquad\text{and}\qquad m\mid R(x),
\]
we have \(a(m)\leq x\). If, in addition, no smaller positive multiple of \(m\) has the corresponding reversal property, then \(a(m)=x\).

We first determine the three values needed for \(n=2,3,4\).

Write the decimal digits of a positive integer in least-significant-first order as
\[
(d_0,d_1,\ldots,d_{r-1}),
\]
so that
\[
 x=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}d_i10^i,
 \qquad 0\leq d_i\leq 9.
\]
Put
\[
 S=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}d_i,
 \qquad W=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}i d_i.
\]
The reversed digit list has weighted sum
\[
 W^{\mathrm{rev}}=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}i d_{r-1-i}.
\]
Changing the index from \(i\) to \(r-1-i\) gives the useful identity
\[
 W+W^{\mathrm{rev}}=(r-1)S. \tag{1}
\]

Since \(10=1+9\), the binomial theorem gives, for every \(i\geq 0\),
\[
 10^i=(1+9)^i\equiv 1+9i\pmod {81}; \tag{2}
\]
all binomial terms of degree at least two contain \(9^2=81\). The same congruence consequently holds modulo \(27\). Therefore, for either \(M=27\) or \(M=81\),
\[
 x\equiv S+9W\pmod M. \tag{3}
\]
Applying the same formula to the reversed list yields
\[
 R(x)\equiv S+9W^{\mathrm{rev}}\pmod M. \tag{4}
\]
If both \(x\) and \(R(x)\) are divisible by \(M\), addition of (3) and (4), followed by (1), shows that
\[
 M\mid 2S+9(r-1)S=(9r-7)S. \tag{5}
\]
The integer \(9r-7\) is congruent to \(-7\) modulo \(3\), so it is relatively prime to every power of \(3\), in particular to \(27\) and \(81\). Thus (5) implies
\[
 M\mid S. \tag{6}
\]

We apply this first with \(M=27\). Suppose that \(0<x<999\), and that both \(x\) and \(R(x)\) are divisible by \(27\). The number \(x\) has at most three decimal digits, so \(r\leq 3\), and hence
\[
 0<S\leq 9r\leq 27.
\]
The strict lower bound holds because \(x>0\), so at least one digit is nonzero. By (6), \(27\mid S\), and therefore \(S=27\). Equality in the bounds above forces \(r=3\) and every digit to equal \(9\). Consequently \(x=999\), contradicting \(x<999\). We have proved that there is no positive admissible multiple of \(27\) below \(999\). On the other hand,
\[
 999=37\cdot 27,
 \qquad R(999)=999,

a number which is also divisible by \(27\). It follows that
\[
 a(27)=999. \tag{7}
\]

The identical argument with \(M=81\) handles nine-digit numbers. If \(0<x<999{,}999{,}999\), then \(x\) has at most nine digits. If both \(x\) and \(R(x)\) are divisible by \(81\), (6) gives \(81\mid S\), while
\[
 0<S\leq 9r\leq 81.
\]
Hence \(S=81\), which forces \(r=9\) and all nine digits to be \(9\). This would make \(x=999{,}999{,}999\), contrary to the strict inequality. Thus no admissible positive multiple of \(81\) is smaller than that number. Since
\[
 999{,}999{,}999=12{,}345{,}679\cdot81

a nd the number is unchanged by decimal reversal, we obtain
\[
 a(81)=999{,}999{,}999. \tag{8}
\]
Finally, \(9\) itself is a multiple of \(9\) and is unchanged by reversal. It is plainly the least positive multiple of \(9\), so
\[
 a(9)=9. \tag{9}
\]

It remains to prove that the proposed equality fails for every \(n\geq5\). We do this by constructing, for each such \(n\), an admissible number much smaller than the all-nines number in the conjectured formula.

Let
\[
 B=10^{10},\qquad
 A=4{,}899{,}999{,}987,
 \qquad C=7{,}899{,}999{,}984.
\]
The ten digits of \(A\), in least-significant-first order, are
\[
 [7,8,9,9,9,9,9,9,8,4].
\]
Reversing this list gives the decimal integer \(C\). In particular, a decimal number made by repeating the ten-digit block of \(A\) reverses to the number made by repeating the ten-digit block of \(C\). Direct integer division gives
\[
 A=3^5\cdot20{,}164{,}609,
 \qquad
 C=3^5\cdot32{,}510{,}288. \tag{10}
\]

For \(T\geq1\), define the geometric sum
\[
 G_T=1+B+B^2+\cdots+B^{T-1}.
\]
Then
\[
 X_T=A G_T \tag{11}
\]
is exactly the decimal integer formed by repeating the ten-digit block \(4899999987\), \(T\) times. There are no carries between blocks because multiplication by \(B=10^{10}\) simply shifts a block ten decimal places. Reversing all \(10T\) digits reverses the order of the blocks and reverses each block. Since every block is the same, the order reversal has no further effect, and therefore
\[
 R(X_T)=C G_T. \tag{12}
\]
The first and last digits of the blocks are nonzero, so these are genuine \(10T\)-digit descriptions and no ambiguity involving leading zeroes occurs.

We need one divisibility fact about the geometric sum:
\[
 3^t\mid G_{3^t}\qquad(t\geq0). \tag{13}
\]
Here the subscript denotes the number of terms, so explicitly
\(G_{3^t}=\sum_{i=0}^{3^t-1}B^i\). This can be proved by induction on \(t\). For \(t=0\), the sum has one term and is \(1\), which is divisible by \(3^0=1\). For the induction step, factor the geometric sum into three consecutive groups:
\[
 G_{3^{t+1}}
 =G_{3^t}\bigl(1+B^{3^t}+B^{2\cdot3^t}\bigr). \tag{14}
\]
Because \(B=10^{10}\equiv1\pmod3\), the second factor in (14) is congruent to \(1+1+1=0\pmod3\). By the induction hypothesis the first factor is divisible by \(3^t\), so their product is divisible by \(3^{t+1}\). This proves (13).

Now fix \(n\geq5\), and put
\[
 t=n-5,
 \qquad T=3^t=3^{n-5},
 \qquad X=X_T.

a nd note that \(T\geq1\). From (10), (11), and (13),
\[
 3^n=3^5\cdot3^{n-5}\mid A G_T=X. \tag{15}
\]
Likewise, using (10), (12), and (13),
\[
 3^n\mid C G_T=R(X). \tag{16}
\]
Thus \(X\) is an admissible positive multiple for the definition of \(a(3^n)\), and consequently
\[
 a(3^n)\leq X. \tag{17}
\]

We next compare its size with the conjectured all-nines number. The repeated-block description has \(10T\) decimal digits, so
\[
 X<10^{10T}. \tag{18}
\]
On the other hand,
\[
 3^{n-2}=3^{(n-5)+3}=27\cdot3^{n-5}=27T. \tag{19}
\]
Because \(T\geq1\),
\[
 10T+1\leq27T.
\]
Also
\[
 10^{10T}+1<10^{10T+1}\leq10^{27T}.
\]
Together with (18), this implies
\[
 X+1<10^{27T},

a nd hence, by (19),
\[
 X<10^{3^{n-2}}-1. \tag{20}
\]
Combining (17) and (20) gives
\[
 a(3^n)<10^{3^{n-2}}-1
 \qquad(n\geq5). \tag{21}
\]
In particular, equality with the proposed value is impossible for every \(n\geq5\).

We can now finish the equivalence. Assume \(n\geq2\). If \(n=2\), then by (9)
\[
 a(3^n)=a(9)=9=10^{3^0}-1=10^{3^{n-2}}-1.
\]
If \(n=3\), then by (7)
\[
 a(3^n)=a(27)=999=10^3-1=10^{3^{n-2}}-1.
\]
If \(n=4\), then by (8)
\[
 a(3^n)=a(81)=999{,}999{,}999=10^9-1=10^{3^{n-2}}-1.
\]
Thus every \(n\in\{2,3,4\}\) gives equality. Conversely, if \(n\geq2\) is not \(2\), \(3\), or \(4\), then necessarily \(n\geq5\), and (21) shows that equality fails. Therefore, for every integer \(n\geq2\),
\[
 a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 n\in\{2,3,4\}.
\]
